Focal neurologic findings and seizures are rare in HACE; their presence should lead to suspicion of an intracranial lesion, a seizure disorder, or hyponatremia. HAPE progresses to dyspnea at rest and frank respiratory distress, often with bloody sputum. This typical progression over 1–2 days is easily recognizable as HAPE, but the condition in those with poor ventilatory response may present only as central nervous system dysfunction, with confusion and drowsiness, while SpO2 is quite low.

In remote areas, initiate descent for anyone suspected of having HACE, in conjunction with dexamethasone and oxygen, if available.
